papers.title: A LoRa-Compatible Receiver with Programmable Noise-Power Trade-Off and Integrated Wake-Up Mode
papers.summary: Programmable receivers allow an optimal performance in the variable conditions of the wireless channel. An extensive analysis of their noise-power trade-off enables the development of a main receiver with embedded wake-up circuitry. This makes the seamless integration of wake-up receivers (WuRXs) in RF receivers possible, avoiding power, area, complexity, and cost overheads in the system. In this paper, we propose the first LoRa-compatible receiver with an integrated wake-up mode and a programmable noise-power trade-off. In main-receiver mode, it consumes 4.57 mW for a sensitivity of -138 dBm, but it can save up to 62.6% of power consumption at the cost of an 8.3-dB sensitivity degradation. In wake-up mode, sensitivity down to -126 dBm is achieved for a 32-ms latency and 1.5 mW of power consumption. The power consumption remains relatively high due to a sub-optimal design of the the phase-locked loop (PLL). In the end, the wake-up mode consumes 3X less than the lowest-noise configuration in main-receiver mode.

papers.title: Digital Twin-Conditioned RSS-Fingerprint Localization in Cell-Free Millimeter-Wave Networks
papers.summary: Digital twins (DTs) can generate dense synthetic fingerprints for localization via ray tracing, yet the sim-to-real domain gap limits their direct use, particularly in cell-free millimeter-wave (mmWave) deployments where distributed geometries and blockage-induced sparsity widen the mismatch. We propose DT-conditioned (DTCond), a framework that fuses real and DT beam-domain fingerprints as complementary inputs through per-domain encoders, learnable per-access point (AP) attention, and calibrated uncertainty. We derive oracle and pipeline Cram\'er-Rao bounds (CRBs) for DT-aided fingerprint localization, proving that DT information strictly tightens the positioning bound whenever spatial structure is preserved, with a heteroscedastic refinement that tightens the bound by a further 9.1%. On a real 28 GHz cell-free testbed, the deployable two-stage pipeline, which reads the DT fingerprint at a coarse k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) estimate, achieves 0.284 m mean error against 0.313 m for real-only k-NN. With the DT fingerprint read at the true position (oracle input), DT conditioning achieves 0.186 m mean error, validated through a ten-method ablation against domain-adaptation (DA) and transfer-learning baselines, and a 48% improvement on unseen regions. Multi-user self-attention provides 31-41% per-user gain for emulated simultaneous users, and progressive calibration reduces the measurement budget by 50%. As a use case, localization drives network configuration in closed loop. Between beam sweeps, a DT updated from measured RSS and read at the tracked position estimate selects the 3 of 81 beam pairs that each AP trains. With 49 calibration anchors in the update, the mean beam-selection loss stays below 1 dB over 2 m of motion, whereas reusing the last sweep loses 2.7 dB after 1 m.

papers.title: Cyclotron: A Recurrence Language for Expressing Interprocessor Communication
papers.summary: We present Cyclotron, a compiler that expresses streaming dataflow algorithms using recurrence equations, which are then compiled to distributed topologies of interlinked processors. Our compiler lowers a language of recurrences over logical iteration spaces into per-processor programs of sends, receives, and computations. In these recurrences, data accesses are not limited to external accesses to memory; data can live separately on the iteration space itself, allowing internal points to communicate values directly with other points. Users specify this communication directly in the recurrence language, which allows them to express various communication patterns such as a nearest-neighbor systolic exchange, a one-to-all broadcast, a bidirectional split ring, or an asymmetric and piecewise broadcast pattern, which are often not supported by standard distributed linear algebra libraries. These recurrences describe the algorithm and communication independently of how they map onto the hardware. A programmer then chooses which dimensions execute across processors and which execute over time, without rewriting the entire program. Users only specify data dependencies across the iteration space, and the compiler safely generates a program, per process, with correct placement of both communication and computational operators according to the chosen space--time mapping. We evaluate distributed matrix multiplication, TRSM, Cholesky, and fused Cholesky--TRSM on up to 16 CPU nodes and 16 GPUs, comparing against ScaLAPACK, SLATE, and cuSolverMp. Cyclotron is competitive with and often outperforms these hand-optimized libraries; for Cholesky, the best communication strategy changes with problem size and architecture.

papers.title: Orientation-Aware Deep Learning Framework for RSSI-Based Indoor Localization in RIS-Aided mmWave Systems
papers.summary: Reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-aided millimeter wave (mmWave) systems provide directional measurements of received power for indoor localization, but device orientation changes the fingerprints. This work proposes an orientation-aware dual-stream gated (O-DSG) deep learning framework for received signal strength indicator (RSSI)-based indoor localization. An orientation classifier estimates device orientation from RSSI, so inference needs only received power. An embedding of the predicted angle and posterior entropy controls feature modulation and soft expert gating. Parallel convolutional and statistical streams are fused through bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) processing and temporal attention. Single-user measurements in an indoor laboratory at 28 GHz under non-line-of-sight (NLoS) conditions yield a median localization error of 0.141 m, a 25.8% improvement over the closest evaluated baseline (supplied with the measured orientation), and 92.3% orientation classification accuracy across four discrete classes. In spatial regions withheld from training, O-DSG has an average median error of 0.247 m, against 0.392 m for a validation-selected sequence model. A separate offline evaluation constructs non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-style power mixtures from the single-user measurements and measures localization accuracy and computational scaling with up to eight emulated users whose power contributions overlap, under the specified mixture model.

papers.title: Where the SRAM Goes: Per-Symbol Attribution of Static Memory in FreeRTOS-C and Embassy-Rust IoT Firmware on a 64 KB RISC-V Microcontroller
papers.summary: Selecting a firmware stack for a memory-constrained microcontroller is usually guided by aggregate binary sizes, which report how much SRAM a build consumes but not where it goes or why. We address that gap with a per-symbol attribution method that decomposes static RAM into architectural categories - scheduler heap, network buffers and pools, task stacks, and linker-reserved regions - by bounding sized ELF symbols to the .data, .bss and .stack section ranges. The method is validated by reconciling every category sum exactly against the size-based totals for all sixteen builds. We apply it to eight cumulative firmware milestones, from a bare task scaffold to a full MQTT-over-Ethernet client, implemented twice, in FreeRTOS-C and in Embassy-Rust, on the CH32V203RBT6, a RISC-V microcontroller with 64 KB SRAM and an on-chip Ethernet MAC and PHY, with functional parity verified on hardware at every milestone. The decomposition shows that both stacks spend a nearly identical share of their RAM on networking (63.8% versus 63.9%), yet the absolute cost differs by 4.4 times: 40,719 bytes for lwIP against 9,316 bytes for smoltcp. FreeRTOS task stacks grow linearly at roughly 1 KB per task while Embassy async state grows with state-machine complexity. We also report that lwIP could not be integrated under an all-static discipline on this platform, requiring a 20 KB arena that smoltcp does not. The measurement harness, the attribution tool, and the sixteen firmware implementations are released as artefacts.

papers.title: Probabilistic Optical-Layer Surrogate for Risk-Aware Control-Plane Decision Making
papers.summary: In this paper, we propose a generative surrogate for the optical layer. Current control-plane decisions in optical transport networks are made using analytical impairment models, deterministic learned predictors, or quantile-regression-based uncertainty estimates. These approaches expose only a limited, static summary of the optical layer at any given time. This forces the control plane to rely on conservative fixed margins that leave capacity underutilized. Our proposed surrogate is a conditional generative model trained on traces from optical simulators with validated physical models. The surrogate produces a full conditional distribution over physical-layer metrics such as OSNR, Q-margin, nonlinear penalty, and feasibility. This output allows the controller to estimate violation probability and tail risk at arbitrary thresholds at runtime. This is different from existing approaches because no retraining is required for each decision. We present the first case study in fast path feasibility estimation using a generative surrogate for the optical layer. We compare the surrogate against simulators, deterministic learned predictors, and quantile-regression estimators. We evaluate the surrogate along nine research questions (RQ1--RQ9) covering prediction accuracy, inference latency, uncertainty quality, controller integration, cross-emulator generalization, dynamic reconfiguration under span degradation, topology scalability, GNPy-validated generalization, and finally, inference latency on real-world live hardware traces. The core contribution is an optical-layer control abstraction where physical-layer behavior is exposed as a fast probabilistic query mechanism instead of an offline simulation output or a deterministic feasibility rule.

papers.title: Helix: A Unified Programmable Accelerator for Diverse Krylov Subspace Solvers
papers.summary: Domain-specific accelerators deliver high performance and energy efficiency through specialization but often lack support for extensible algorithm families. Existing FPGA accelerators for Krylov subspace methods, which iteratively solve sparse linear systems, typically support a single solver or require separate hardware configurations. Helix follows a systematic algorithm-family design methodology that first abstracts common computational primitives from diverse Krylov solvers and builds the architecture around efficient, programmable primitive kernels. Helix then introduces programmable datapaths to coordinate these primitives. Its architecture decouples hardware implementation from solver-specific execution, enabling HBM reuse and zero solver-switching latency. Finally, Helix provides a DSL compiler that efficiently maps different solvers onto the architecture while optimizing vector-operation performance for each solver. We prototype Helix on a Xilinx Alveo U55C FPGA and evaluate Helix's practicality and performance by using it to compile and execute eight solvers. Helix achieves up to 7.91x and 1.16x speedups over Xilinx XcgSolver and the state-of-the-art FPGA accelerator Callipepla, respectively, both of which support only JPCG. Across the eight solvers, Helix sustains 47.5% - 96.9% of the throughput of an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU while delivering 2.29x - 4.66x higher energy efficiency and 1.89x - 3.85x higher throughput per unit peak memory bandwidth. The programmable components incur 0.25% - 0.57% execution-time overhead and 4.7% LUT and 4.0% FF overhead, demonstrating negligible overhead for programmability.

papers.title: Normalization by Evaluation with Substitutions as Operations
papers.summary: In previous works on normalization by evaluation (NbE) with an untyped domain model, explicit substitutions are a major decision choice, which, in retrospect, is taken to simplify subsequent semantic proofs. This choice hence is taken for a purely technical reason. In addition, there is no obvious lemma to test the completeness of the definition or the laws for explicit substitutions. In this technical report, we investigate NbE in a typical setting, i.e. defining substitutions as operations. We show that this setting brings simplifications in proving syntactic properties and soundness of NbE, though complications are introduced in the completeness proof of NbE.

papers.title: Coordination-Free Workload Regularization for Variable-Cost Distributed Training
papers.summary: Synchronous data-parallel training usually assigns every rank the same number of records, even when record costs vary by orders of magnitude. For variable-length models, this converts input variation into idle time because each step waits for its most expensive rank-local batch. We present Batch Cost Lookahead (BCL), a coordination-free data-loading policy that buffers a bounded rank-local window and repartitions it into fixed-cardinality packs with balanced estimated cost. BCL preserves the trainer's record-count contract and requires neither cross-rank metadata exchange nor runtime modification. In simulation over public workload distributions, enabling BCL reduces per-rank estimated batch-cost variability by up to 82.8%. Across 13 NeMo-RL SFT corpora on eight H200 GPUs, rank-local BCL runs 1.050 to 1.167 times faster than pooled MFFD. Compiled H200 measurements on an internal sequence workload show speedups of 1.197 to 1.343 times over packed execution from one to four nodes. We also identify a memory-feasibility boundary: a p99 cap for high-variance or OOM-prone data bounds outliers before BCL balances the rest. These results show that substantial variable-cost imbalance can be removed at the data-loader boundary, while clarifying when data preparation or broader coordination is still necessary.

papers.title: Range: Decoupling KV-Cache Reuse Granularity from Storage Work
papers.summary: LLM serving reuses cached key-value (KV) state to skip prefill, and growing contexts push that state past GPU HBM and CPU DRAM onto NVMe SSDs, placing prefix restore on the critical path of time-to-first-token (TTFT). We find that on a well-configured host-issued path the SSD is not the bottleneck: restoring the same 6 GiB of KV takes 2.1 s as 192 objects but 3.0 s as 6,144 objects, and more under layerwise loading, because every layer of the storage stack - lookup, allocation, I/O submission, GPU delivery, store, index - charges per logical object while the bytes stay the same. This cost grows with the KV footprint: longer contexts, deeper models under layerwise loading, and tensor parallelism each multiply the object count. Prior systems move this per-object work from the CPU to the GPU; the work remains per object. This paper presents Range, a KV-cache storage engine for vLLM and LMCache built on one principle: every cost on the storage path scales with bytes or physical batches, never with logical objects. Range tickets replace per-key lookup and ownership with token metadata and physical leases; byte stripes make the on-media layout independent of reuse granularity; completion-owned GPU transfer banks batch delivery and extraction and release each layer to attention as it lands. Range keeps the kernel cuFile path and changes four lines of vLLM. On a fixed 6 GiB restore, Range's median TTFT stays at 1.79-1.80 s across a 32x range of object counts and under layerwise delivery, within 70 ms of the prefix already being resident in GPU memory, while tuned in-process LMCache rises from 2.12 s to 3.01 s. Range improves on the fastest multiprocess DRAM-bounced path by 0.44 s at coarse granularity while moving no payload through host memory, and holds layerwise reuse at the cost of coarse-grained reuse, where the best stock path takes 2.24 s.

papers.title: Characterizing Predictability-Latency Trade-offs of KV-Cache SSD Offloading in LMCache for LLM Serving Systems
papers.summary: KV-cache offload is widely used to stretch GPU memory for LLM serving, but its storage behavior has not been characterized at the block-device level. In this paper, we study LMCache through realworld multi-session workloads that span same/different context x same/different prompt, using over 100 stateless requests per workload. Our comparison is observational rather than factorial: it contrasts two realizable deployment snapshots -- LMCache 0.3.0 with buffered I/O and the kernel page cache, and LMCache 0.3.16 with prefix-aware deduplication and O_DIRECT. Key findings define the paper. First, the legacy stack appears almost read-free at the SSD layer in all four workloads, but a flush_ram experiment shows that this is conditional on page-cache warmth: once the cache is evicted, the same path issues about 1 GB of sequential reads in 683 ms. Second, deduplication delivers a dramatic write reduction only for the exact-repeat workload: one set collapses from 1.62 GB to 11.75 MB of writes, while the other three sets remain in the 2-5 GB range. Third, O_DIRECT converts a hidden and bimodal read cost into an explicit and stable one: on one set, warm TTFT rises from 27 ms to 93 ms because each of the 99 warm requests re-reads the same ~12 MB partial chunk from SSD. The main conclusion is therefore not "newer is better," but a system trade-off: predictability versus average-case latency.

papers.title: PSA: A Pruning-Friendly Sparse-Aware Accelerator for Efficient Sparse Convolution in SNNs
papers.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient artificial intelligence due to their event-driven sparse computation, and neuron pruning can further reduce redundant operations. However, in practical hardware accelerators, spike sparsity and pruning-induced sparsity produce highly irregular sparse workloads that are difficult to execute efficiently. Existing approaches do not jointly support sparse-input execution, low-overhead sparse convolution lowering and pruning-friendly execution. This paper presents PSA, a Pruning-friendly Sparse-aware Accelerator for efficient sparse convolution in SNNs. PSA features a Sparse-Aware Merge-Accumulation (SAMA) dataflow that aligns sparse spike indices and converts irregular activations into continuous computation streams for efficient sparse convolution execution. It further introduces a Sparse Implicit Group-wise im2col (SIG-im2col) convolution lowering mechanism that converts sparse convolution into SpMM on-chip with low mapping cost and memory overhead. In addition, PSA integrates a lightweight pruning-friendly gating mechanism to directly support pruned SNNs. Results on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 show that PSA achieves a 4.45x improvement in energy efficiency and an 18.52x reduction in energy-delay product (EDP) over the dense baseline.

papers.title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed at the edge to support complex tasks that require collaboration and information exchange among multiple agents. However, when task contexts are passed across agents, shared context that has already been processed by upstream agents often needs to be prefilled again, resulting in substantial redundant computation. Reusing an already prefilled key--value (KV) cache can avoid this recomputation, but requires the reusable KV state to be transferred across the network before the receiving agent can begin generation. Under strict time-to-first-token (TTFT) deadlines and unreliable edge links, delivering the complete KV cache may be infeasible, making it necessary to prioritize and protect the most valuable KV information within a limited transmission budget. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that jointly exploits model-side KV importance and transport-side reliability. PriorityFEC first constructs a utility-aware source stream by placing high-utility KV blocks at earlier transmission positions. It then protects the ordered stream using a feedback-adaptive Streaming Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) mechanism, which schedules repair packets according to receiver feedback before the TTFT deadline. We implement PriorityFEC on a distributed edge LLM serving prototype and evaluate it with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets. Results show that PriorityFEC achieves superior task quality over the compared transport schemes, with its advantages becoming particularly pronounced under stringent deadline constraints. These results demonstrate the importance of jointly optimizing KV-cache utility and deadline-aware transport reliability when reusable LLM state must be handed off across unreliable edge networks.

papers.title: When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill
papers.summary: Reusing the attention KV cache across requests is a standard way to cut prefill cost in long-context LLM serving, and production systems increasingly back the per-engine cache with a remote tier shared by every engine. We study such a tier in a disaggregated deployment of GLM-5.3, an FP8 mixture-of-experts model with multi-head latent attention (MLA), on 8xB300 nodes running prefill context parallelism (PCP8). Enabling the remote tier (LMCache with a Valkey store) left median time-to-first-token unchanged but raised the 16k-token p99 from 3.96 s to 17.3 s. Replaying a production request stream on an isolated engine, we find that a remote hit took 0.88 s against 0.31 s to recompute the prompt, and that synchronous loading turned a hit-heavy stream into an unstable queue: p99 83.32 s with the GPUs 7% busy. A two-term cost model explains both: a hit pays off only if the tier delivers more than B* = sR (2.53 GB/s for this model and GPU), and a fixed per-hit engine cost (T0 ~ 0.33 s) means that hits on prompts shorter than about 17k tokens cannot beat recompute at any bandwidth. Guided by the model, we (i) shard the MLA KV store across PCP ranks, with a proof that the existing minimum-over-ranks lookup returns the longest cached prefix and a load protocol that can never desynchronize collectives; (ii) partition the remote tier by rank, one server instance per rank with no coordination, which raises GET bandwidth 6.3x to 10.76 GB/s; (iii) add asynchronous loading to the sharded store; and (iv) fix three client bugs that caused unbounded stalls. On the hit-heavy stream, with 98.5% of prompt tokens served from the remote tier, p99 falls from 83.32 s to 0.67 s. The sharded store raises prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% together with an upstream kernel fix. All changes are submitted upstream to LMCache.

papers.title: Minimum RISC-V: Maximum FPGA Efficiency
papers.summary: RISC-V processors are now widely available for FPGAs, with most FPGA vendors replacing their proprietary soft-CPU architectures with this instruction-set architecture (ISA). Although contemporary FPGAs are increasingly resource- and feature-rich, a soft processor system---including memory---often occupies a disproportionately large footprint and delivers only modest performance relative to the potential of the target device. In this work we first design a lightweight but deeply pipelined RISC-V core that can run above 700 MHz in a mid-range device and that is capable of retiring one instruction per clock under ideal conditions. We then develop and demonstrate a new optimization method that compiles the final application binary and a specialized processor instance contemporaneously. The method expands each instruction into an application-specific encoding, removes unused datapath and decode logic during synthesis, and yields cores that remain assembler-compatible with the original program while no longer being binary-compatible with a general-purpose RISC-V. We implement example designs on RV32I (base integer), RV32M (integer multiply), and RV32F (single-precision floating-point) configurations. Our optimized RISC-V is as small as 170 ALMs and closes timing at 775 MHz in an Altera Agilex-5 device. Finally, we show that these processors can be packed into a deterministic area and stepped-and-repeated continuously without material impact on performance, enabling predictable multi-core density planning.

papers.title: Independent Data-Integrity Verification for LLM-Driven Functional Coverage Closure in Hardware Design
papers.summary: LLM agents can write directed tests that close functional coverage, but coverage only shows that a state was reached, not that the data on the way there was correct. This is a long-known point in verification and we do not claim it as new. We describe a small coverage-closure agent that applies it to an LLM loop: coverage is read from the report that the simulation itself exports (cocotb-coverage YAML) and never taken from the model's account, and data integrity is checked by scoreboards that are separate from the model. On three architecturally distinct RTL designs (an asynchronous FIFO, a UART transmitter and an AHB2APB bridge) the agent raised coverage from 91.7%, 88.9% and 67.4% to 100% within its 8-iteration budget in every logged run, using one design-agnostic agent. A reactive scoreboard monitor attached to the FIFO's base testbench also found a clock-domain-crossing bug in the author's own stimulus code. The monitor is not yet attached to the LLM-generated tests, so their data integrity is not independently checked; one manual check on a single FIFO test is reported as preliminary. We list the weaknesses of this evidence: three designs, no baseline, no ablation, and logged runs that come from several agent checkpoints.

papers.title: Decoding What iOS Location Services Send to Apple: An LLM Is an Unreliable Analyst but a Useful Toolmaker
papers.summary: Reverse engineering the data formats used by mobile software is skilled and slow, and using AI to assist with it is attractive. We evaluate this for the protobuf messages that an iPhone sends to Apple's location services. Working from Apple's binaries, we use two frontier models (Claude Opus 4.8, Codex GPT Sol 5.6) to reconstruct the schemas of protobufs observed in network traffic. The great majority of the schemas contain substantial errors, and these are hard to detect because the schemas are internally consistent. Direct AI use is therefore unsuitable for forensic and privacy analysis. AI can, however, write reliable analysis tools when their output can be validated. We use Claude to write a Python tool, Extractor, that reliably recovers protobuf schemas from Apple binaries. We validate it against binaries compiled from schemas with known answers, previously published schemas, and network measurements. We demonstrate the use of Extractor to decode and analyse the location services network traffic of a jailbroken iPhone 8 (iOS 16.7.11).

papers.title: Exact Makespan Bounds and the GPipe Homogeneity Bias for Heterogeneous LLM Inference Pipelines
papers.summary: We give an exact critical-path characterization of the makespan of micro-batch pipelines serving LLMs on heterogeneous GPU clusters, quantifying how the classic homogeneous GPipe formula errs. In the pure-forward, communication-free, infinite-buffer setting, T(M) = (M-1)tau_max + Sum_j tau_j, where tau_j is stage j's per-micro-batch service time and M the micro-batch count (Theorem 1). Under asynchronous communication -- modern NCCL-based serving -- it extends to T(M) = Sum_j tau_j + Sum_j d_j + (M-1)tau_max, with Sum_j d_j a purely additive constant (Theorem 2); under blocking communication, T(M) = (M-1)sigma_max + Sum_s sigma_s with sigma_s = tau_s + d_s, so communication enters the steady-state slope iff some d_s > tau_max - tau_s (Theorem 3). These results quantify the GPipe overestimate, decompose the bias into a homogeneity term Sum_j (tau_max - tau_j) and a communication-ignoring term Sum_j d_j, and imply that balancing per-stage compute dominates communication reduction for steady-state throughput. A real system with partial overlap is sandwiched between Theorems 2 and 3, with a closed-form bound on the overlap throughput gain. All claims are validated pointwise (error < 10^-9) on eleven configurations and a 1.6x10^5-point fuzz, including a mixed RTX 5090/3090/GTX 1070 partition. We situate the results in flow-shop scheduling and list open extensions: bandwidth-limited communication, bounded buffers, prefill-decode interleaving.

papers.title: Compiling Multi-Threshold Operators for Quantized Non-Monotonic and Fine-Granular Activations in Custom-Tailored DNN Accelerators
papers.summary: Aggressive quantization of neural networks can expose activation functions as bottlenecks for efficient hardware acceleration. Implementing quantized activations as multi-threshold operations has been shown to be a promising optimization, allowing for efficient hardware implementation of few-bit activations. However, current implementations are limited to monotonically increasing functions, quantization schemes with one-dimensional (per-channel) granularity and a small set of predefined activation-quantizer combinations. We formalize the multi-threshold representation to extend it to non-monotonic functions and fine-granular parameters, i.e., multi-dimensional thresholds. For automated conversion of quantized function compositions into threshold representation, we propose a systematic approach via algebraic rules integrated into the ONNX-based compiler infrastructure. We experimentally validate our solution on a selection of monotonic and non-monotonic functions by extending the binary search based multi-threshold operator that is integrated into the FINN framework for end-to-end synthesis of custom-tailored FPGA accelerators. The cost of hardware support for non-monotonicity and fine-granularity is characterized in comparison to an alternative approach utilizing existing operators via graph-level decomposition. We compare our method to prior work as well as the approach taken by the hls4ml framework. As an outlook, we demonstrate the prospects of using the multi-threshold representation during the training of a neural network as a form of quantization aware training.

papers.title: Resource-aware Sub-network Allocation for Heterogeneous Decentralized Learning
papers.summary: System heterogeneity in computation, communication, and memory can substantially limit synchronous decentralized learning, where each training round is constrained by resource-limited nodes. Existing approaches provide limited support for jointly determining node-specific model capacities from deployment resources. We propose RASA-DL, a resource-aware sub-network allocation framework that treats the maximum sub-network width assigned to each node as a deployment variable. RASA-DL combines offline hardware profiling of computation and memory costs with deployment-aware profiling of learning utility under heterogeneous decentralized training. Using these profiles together with node- and link-level resource information, we formulate deployment as a bottleneck-latency minimization problem subject to per-node memory constraints and a required aggregate learning utility. Exploiting the monotone feasibility of the latency threshold, RASA-DL efficiently identifies the deployment through a binary-search-based allocation procedure. Experiments under controlled resource heterogeneity demonstrate favorable accuracy--latency tradeoffs. Under the Moderate and Severe regimes, the minimum-latency operating point improves accuracy over the largest globally feasible uniform deployment by 2.80 and 2.43 percentage points, respectively, at the same modeled round latency. The advantage is further amplified under strong Non-IID data heterogeneity.

papers.title: ETH: Data-Balanced Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism for Training Large Models
papers.summary: Current heterogeneity-aware training systems for large models balance workloads by assigning unequal numbers of layers across pipeline stages, a strategy aimed at equalizing execution time through a unique pipeline configuration. However, this approach fails to address critical memory constraints and suffers from inherently coarse balancing granularity. In this paper, we propose Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism (HPP), a novel approach enabling efficient and fine-grained data balance across heterogeneous pipelines. To address HPP's key challenges, prohibitive search overhead for optimal configurations and high communication overhead from asymmetric All-Reduce, we design the ETH training system. ETH employs a hierarchical workload balance framework that jointly optimizes balance across heterogeneous pipelines and within individual pipeline stages. To mitigate asymmetric communication costs, ETH implements block-wise gradient aggregation. Furthermore, it integrates specialized optimizations that dramatically reduce HPP configuration search overhead. Evaluations demonstrate ETH achieves up to 2x training speedup while reducing configuration generation overhead by up to 56x compared to state-of-the-art systems. The code is available at https://github.com/YuMJie/ETH.

papers.title: Coverage-Preserving Self-Healing in Partially Observable 3D UAV Swarm Networks via an Advection-Diffusion Graph Transformer
papers.summary: This paper investigates the resilience and self-healing of unmanned aerial vehicle swarm communication networks under severe network partitioning in complex and adversarial environments. To address limited global observability after damage, we develop a damage-state inference mechanism that enables the ground control station (GCS) to infer global failures from sparse local reports without transmitting location-sensitive coordinates. To recover multi-cluster partitioned topologies, we then propose AdDiff-GT, a physics-inspired graph Transformer that incorporates advection-diffusion dynamics into a node-supernode hybrid graph. Local message propagation captures intra-cluster structural relationships, while global attention models inter-cluster interactions. A weighted composite loss jointly considers connectivity restoration, maneuvering cost, motion consistency, inter-cluster coordination, and spatial preservation during model training. We further develop a meta-learning strategy for transferable initialization across damage patterns and swarm scales, enabling efficient online GCS adaptation and distributed airborne inference. Simulations on 8,000 partitioned scenarios, including 5,000 large-scale cases, show that AdDiff-GT achieves effective topology recovery and spatial preservation over six representative baselines. Meta-learning reduces online planning overhead with a minor increase in recovery steps, balancing prior knowledge transfer and online adaptation.

papers.title: Efficient KV Cache Migration for Geo-Distributed LLM Inference in Collaborative Edge Computing
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown exceptional capabilities but rely heavily on centralized cloud GPU clusters, leading to high bandwidth costs, latency, and privacy issues. Edge computing offers a solution by deploying LLMs closer to users on edge servers, yet single edge servers often cannot meet LLMs' heavy computational demands. Collaborative Edge Computing (CEC) addresses this challenge by integrating resources of multiple geo-distributed heterogeneous edge servers, which jointly host small model shards and associated Key-Value (KV) cache for distributed inference. However, edge servers may disconnect or easily become overloaded, making it essential to migrate stateful KV cache to other servers for ensuring continuous service. Existing cloud-based KV cache management methods, such as direct cross-GPUs transmission and recomputation from input tokens are ill-suited for bandwidth-constrained and resource-limited edge environments. In this work, we propose EdgeFlow, a novel hybrid KV cache migration scheme that integrates direct KV cache transmission with activation-based recomputation, leveraging parallel computation and communication to minimize migration time. On this basis, we formulate a multi-node KV migration optimization problem and design a 2-approximation algorithm based on improved linear programming relaxation and bipartite graph techniques. Extensive experiments on a real-world distributed LLM inference platform demonstrate that EdgeFlow reduces migration time by up to 45%, significantly enhancing the robustness and efficiency of distributed LLM inference in collaborative edge computing.

papers.title: Architecting for Hardware Diversity: Meta's End-to-End Co-Design for High-Performance AI Training on AMD GPUs
papers.summary: Meta deploys a heterogeneous fleet comprising NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and proprietary MTIA accelerators to reduce costs and mitigate vendor lock-in. However, the extensive history of NVIDIA-specific optimizations hinders performance portability to other hardware. This paper presents our methods for optimizing alternative accelerators, using AMD Instinct MI350X versus NVIDIA B200 for recommendation model training as a case study. We propose three reusable principles. First, hardware-model co-design is essential: rather than directly porting models from NVIDIA GPUs, revising model structures and software recipes allows full exploitation of accelerator-specific strengths (e.g., MI350X's 1.6x HBM capacity relative to B200). Second, our analytical performance model enables zero-warmup optimal kernel selection across diverse datatypes and matrix shapes in production models, drastically simplifying tuning. Third, increasingly mature agentic workflows have lowered the barrier to porting from the CUDA ecosystem; we extend these workflows for microarchitecture-aware kernel optimizations and custom shim generation. Compared to the directly ported baseline, these methods deliver up to 1.5x improvement in end-to-end training throughput. To our knowledge, this is the first hyperscaler report on productionizing AMD GPUs for large-scale training. Our contributions have been upstreamed to the open-source PyTorch, Triton, and ROCm ecosystems.

papers.title: Online Tree Caching
papers.summary: We initiate the study of a natural and practically relevant new variant of online caching where the to-be-cached items can have dependencies. We assume that the universe is a tree $T$ and items are tree nodes; we require that if a node $v$ is cached then the whole subtree $T(v)$ rooted at $v$ is cached as well. This theoretical problem finds an immediate application in the context of forwarding table optimization in IP routing and software-defined networks. We present an elegant online deterministic algorithm TC for this problem, and rigorously prove that its competitive ratio is $O(\mathrm{height}(T) \cdot k_{\mathrm{ONL}}/(k_{\mathrm{ONL}}-k_{\mathrm{OPT}}+1))$, where $k_{\mathrm{ONL}}$ and $k_{\mathrm{OPT}}$ denote the cache sizes of an online and the optimal offline algorithm, respectively. The result is optimal up to a factor of $O(\mathrm{height}(T))$. We complement the theoretical analysis with an empirical study on synthetic workloads and CAIDA backbone traffic, illustrating the trade-off between hit rate and cache-update cost.

papers.title: Harnessing MPI mutations for AI error detection
papers.summary: MPI errors are challenging to identify despite the significant number of expert verification tools. Dynamic tools (i.e., requiring profiling) are computationally expensive and accurate in error detection, whereas static analysis (i.e., operating at source code or compilation) is computationally cheap but less accurate. Interestingly, the recent success of AI and LLMs offers an alternative to increase static analysis accuracy while preserving its low overhead. Yet current methods remain difficult to benchmark, too general, and poorly adapted to the specific challenges of high-performance computing. In this paper, we investigate how AI-powered tools can efficiently and accurately detect errors in real-world MPI applications. We propose a novel MPI Mutated Dataset (MMD), constructed from MPI programs extracted from thousands of open-source GitHub projects. After sorting and filtering these files, we inject errors that realistically emulate developers' mistakes using synthetic code mutations. We leverage the dataset to train different AI models and assess their generalization capabilities against standard verification tools. We train compact multilayer perceptrons (MLP) with AST-T5 embeddings (i.e., transformer only encoder network) to detect diverse MPI errors (from the MPI-BugBench (MBB) classification) including CallOrdering or InvalidParameter, achieving detection accuracies up to 92.0%. In some cases, our method outperforms the expert prompted Qwen-3 Coder LLM and provides competitive results compared to established dynamic verification tools. We further evaluate Claude Sonnet 4.5 across different prompting strategies, showing that engineered prompts improve InvalidParam detection accuracy from 84.8% to 93.6%, surpassing the dynamic tool ITAC (87.0%). The full agentic pipeline achieves 73.9% overall multi-class accuracy and 87.6% bug detection recall on MBB. This paves the way for large-scale verification efforts that can use our dataset as a foundation to thoroughly investigate each MPI error in real world applications.

papers.title: Foundations of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts
papers.summary: Microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre and Meltdown undermine security by exploiting software-visible side effects of microarchitectural optimizations like caches and speculative execution. To use modern hardware securely, programmers must take into account the security implications of these optimizations. Yet instruction set architectures (ISAs)---the conventional abstraction layer between hardware and software---are ill-suited for secure programming: by design, they abstract from microarchitectural details and therefore fail to reflect their security consequences. A new security abstraction is emerging to fill this void: hardware-software leakage contracts. To support the principled development of secure software on modern hardware such contracts characterize side-channel leakage at the ISA level. Thereby they enable programmers and compilers to generate code that is provably resistant to side-channel attacks---without having to explicitly reason about the microarchitecture. On the other hand, they provide a specification for hardware designers to ensure that microarchitectures do not introduce unintended and undocumented side channels. This paper introduces the foundations of this emerging topic, discussing recent contributions and unresolved challenges along the way.

papers.title: PAGE404: Breaking GPU Isolation Through Hardware-assisted Page Migration
papers.summary: NVIDIA's Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip represents a new generation of heterogeneous computing, tightly integrating a 72-core Arm-based CPU with a Hopper GPU on a single module via a high-bandwidth, cache-coherent interconnect. By eliminating the conventional PCIe bottleneck for CPU-GPU data movement, this design establishes a unified memory domain that scales to the capacities demanded by generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The architecture also introduces hardware-assisted page migration: driven by access counters, the system dynamically promotes frequently accessed pages from host CPU memory to GPU DRAM to improve memory locality. We study the security of this emerging architecture against new side- and covert-channel attacks targeting its page migration support. We analyze counter-driven migration across both the hardware mechanisms and the UVM driver's interrupt-handling pipeline, and identify two side-channel vulnerabilities: one rooted in the shared structure of access counters, and the other in the driver's response to migration interrupts. We further show that both channels are exploitable across Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions, a feature intended to provide strong, hardware-enforced isolation between co-located tenants. Using proof-of-concept attacks, we build covert channels that reach roughly 8,500 bits per second through eviction-based signaling and 8,100 bits per second through migration-delay-based signaling across MIG instances. The interrupt-based channel also fingerprints inference workloads across distinct large language models (LLMs) and CPU SPEC2017 benchmarks, and estimates the prompt length processed during LLM inference with high accuracy. These results expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and call into question the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.

papers.title: Practical wavelength selection for quantum-augmented networks over shared optical fiber
papers.summary: In a quantum augmented network, sharing optical fiber with classical traffic requires quantum wavelength selection to balance logical fidelity, block acceptance, and classical data reception. Here we develop a wavelength-selection framework for an error-corrected three-stage quantum communication protocol. Under a thermal-background model with independent errors, an ideal one-photon receiver, and ideal recovery, we derive an accepted qubit channel and a key-independent lower bound on logical entanglement fidelity. Combining this bound with block acceptance gives an entanglement-fidelity yield bound, which we maximize over evaluated wavelengths subject to fidelity and classical link-budget requirements. For the Steane [[7,1,3]] code at 5 km per traversal and -10 dBm per classical channel, the largest fidelity certificate occurs near 1537 nm, whereas the largest yield bound occurs near 1551 nm. Along the 1.25 Gb/s classical link budget with 0.2% base error, the optimized yield bound falls below 10^-6 near 10 km per traversal, while fidelity remains certified at 0.99 or higher at longer spans. These results distinguish fidelity and yield constraints and identify certified operating regions for quantum-augmented networks sharing optical fiber.

papers.title: AdaBool: Sparse Boolean Matrix Processing with Adaptive Data Representation
papers.summary: Many data processing tasks revolve around determining whether logical relationships exist between two sets of entities, a pattern that can be naturally modeled as Sparse Boolean Matrix Multiplication (SpBMM). Under Boolean semantics, matrix representations no longer need to store numerical values and instead focus on encoding the positions of non-zero elements, making it highly amenable to data compression for substantially lower memory access overhead. The key challenge, however, is that the most effective compression depends heavily on sparsity distribution: different methods perform best at different sparsity levels, while real-world matrices often contain sharply varying sparsity across regions. Consequently, forcing the entire matrix into any fixed, monolithic representation leaves considerable optimization opportunities untapped. We present AdaBool, a SpBMM framework designed to reconcile this tension through an adaptive data representation. AdaBool partitions matrices into fine-grained element blocks and represents each block with the encoding best matched to its local sparsity. On top of this adaptive encoding, AdaBool introduces a heterogeneous GPU execution model that groups blocks by encoding type and maps them to matching processing paths, enabling efficient execution and scheduling across GPU resources. We implement AdaBool end to end with low-level system optimizations, evaluate it on both production and public workloads, and show that it outperforms representative baselines by over an order of magnitude.

papers.title: A Black-Box Positioning Solution for Effortless Integration in Wearable Navigation
papers.summary: Accurate localization is critical for a wide range of applications, including navigation, augmented reality, safety management, and healthcare. However, achieving accurate positioning remains challenging, especially in GPS-degraded environments. Pedestrian Dead Reckoning (PDR), which estimates position based on inertial sensor data, offers a promising alternative but typically demands substantial effort in algorithm design and system integration. This complexity often leads to prolonged development timelines and elevated costs. To address these challenges, we present the PDR Sensor (PDRS), a plug-and-play, black-box PDR module optimized for seamless integration into wearable and IoT platforms. PDRS integrates a microprocessor and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) within a compact, low-power module. It executes real-time sensor fusion onboard, providing position updates via standard interfaces (I2C, SPI, UART). Experimental evaluations demonstrate its high robustness, achieving a step detection error of just 0.16% over 1250 steps and a traveled distance error of 1.87% under diverse conditions. The system further exhibits low latency (2.5 ms) and modest power consumption (52.35 mA). Unlike conventional studies, the PDRS leverages a holistic co-design of hardware and software to enhance performance and integration aspects, simplifying adoption without requiring deep expertise. By lowering technical barriers, PDRS enables developers and researchers to prioritize innovation in IoT and wearable technologies, accelerating prototyping, reducing development time, and advancing industry progress. Future work aims to enhance accuracy, reduce power usage and module size, and integrate AI-driven techniques to better mitigate drift.

papers.title: HyCo: Hybrid Drafting for Cost-Efficient Mobile-Cloud Speculative Decoding
papers.summary: Device-cloud speculative decoding reduces server computation, but growing a deep draft tree with a small language model (SLM) requires repeated passes on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). We present HyCo, which assigns depth to the server model's native multi-token prediction (MTP) head, executed on the device, and alternative branches to one SLM pass. The server returns the hidden state, input embedding, and key-value entries needed by the head instead of executing its sequential steps. Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU. An {\epsilon}-threshold rule additionally relaxes exact preservation of the verifier's sampling distribution. In single-client runs with a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, HyCo reduces server GPU time per output token relative to server-side MTP self-speculation by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization. With the same acceptance rule, three Spec-Bench runs per system show 9.0 percentage points more saving and 1.9x delivery speed than an SLM-only drafter. HyCo differs from Cloud+MTP by +0.2 judge-score points (paired 95% CI: -0.9 to +1.3); exploratory translation favors SpecEdge-{\epsilon}. Without relaxation, HyCo exact saves 27.7% and 11.9% on the two datasets.

papers.title: Benchmarking Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation in S3-Compatible Object Storage under Client Concurrency
papers.summary: Data encrypted today with classical public-key algorithms could be decrypted once large quantum computers exist. Cloud object stores keep data for years, so the client-side encryption that protects it must move to post-quantum algorithms such as ML-KEM, which adds a key-encapsulation step and a larger ciphertext to every stored object. So far, the cost of ML-KEM has been measured for the algorithm on its own and for securing network connections, but not for encrypting each object in a storage system that serves many clients at once. It has therefore been unclear whether ML-KEM slows such a system, under which conditions, and why. We address this problem by measuring per-object ML-KEM against classical key exchange on an S3-compatible object store, with two client implementations, two processor types and up to 500 concurrent workers, using pre-registered experiments and statistical equivalence tests. ML-KEM reduced throughput only when the client's processor was at or near full load, with one unexplained exception, and then by 4.0 to 4.9% in our main client. Controlled experiments on one processor type traced most of that loss to the way the software library was called, and a second, native client showed that the size of the loss depends on the implementation. The lasting cost is storage: 1,056 more bytes per object than with classical key exchange. The results cover two clients, one single-node store and one cloud provider.

papers.title: ReFlow: Replay-Driven Decoupling for Efficient RL Post-Training
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been a critical paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) reasoning and agentic capabilities, but its efficiency remains a major bottleneck. Existing RL systems commonly rely on asynchronous execution to overlap rollout generation with policy optimization for enhanced efficiency. However, this approach faces inherent limitations: mild policy staleness offers only limited training efficiency gains, whereas aggressive asynchrony can degrade model quality and yields diminishing efficiency gains. The dynamic nature of LLM RL and multi-turn agentic workloads further challenges RL system design, as resource demands shift over time, making static resource allocation and generation strategy inefficient. This paper presents ReFlow, a system-algorithm co-designed RL framework for efficient LLM post-training. Its key insight is that, unlike existing RL frameworks which consume each trajectory only once, experience replay of recent trajectories enables effective sample reuse, thereby amortizing the high cost of rollout generation without incurring excessive policy staleness. To fully exploit this opportunity, ReFlow adopts a decoupled and adaptive architecture with three key designs: a dual replay data cycle supports efficient experience reuse while balancing training throughput and optimization stability; an elastic resource pool enables dynamic resource placement to accommodate evolving RL workloads; an adaptive scheduler coordinates generation strategies and resource allocation to improve resource utilization and boost generation throughput. Experiments across representative single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic RL tasks show that ReFlow improves training throughput by up to $2.06\times$ over state-of-the-art synchronous and asynchronous RL systems, while maintaining comparable or better model performance.

papers.title: Local Epochs as Optimal Stopping: Theory and Evidence in Federated Learning
papers.summary: How long should each client train before communicating? Federated learning usually answers with a fixed, hand-tuned number of local epochs, yet an extra epoch helps only while the loss it removes outweighs the client drift it adds. We cast local training as finite-horizon optimal stopping: a client trains while the next epoch's expected loss reduction exceeds its priced squared drift. We prove that this one-stage look-ahead threshold is optimal whenever stopping decisions are nested, derive closed forms for geometric and power-law returns, and show that an estimated rule loses utility only through wrong-signed decisions. Epoch-level evidence supports the model's structure (geometric diminishing returns and additive drift) and reveals a simple regularity: the stage of training, not the client, sets the budget. The resulting rule, FedStop, is never more than one point below tuned FedAvg in mean accuracy. Where its budgets vary, it raises worst-decile accuracy by 4-8 points over tuned FedAvg and an adaptive-interval baseline, and every one of these gains remains significant after a Holm correction. Against the client-side stopping rules ALT and FLASH, it has the highest CIFAR-10 worst decile on every seed and is level elsewhere. It stays stable where per-client early stopping collapses, and each stopping decision takes constant time.

papers.title: FAOPs: Normal Forms and an Algebra for AI Agent Workflows
papers.summary: Organizations increasingly encode operational procedures as multi-step agent skills, here called Agent Operating Procedures (AOPs), that must be traceable, auditable, reproducible, access-controlled, and bounded in time and cost, requirements that regulated sectors make mandatory. Yet AOPs are typically kept as coarse-grained files, in which steps bundle actions, copied procedures drift apart, any step may reach any tool, and refactoring goes unchecked. We present Functional Agent Operating Procedures (FAOP), a formal theory that brings database-grade discipline to AI agent workflows. FAOP recasts each workflow as a typed function over scoped state and subjects an entire library to four progressive normal forms: Decomposed (FNF-1) splits a workflow into atomic steps, Typed (FNF-2) makes its data flow explicit and type-checked, Factored (FNF-3) gives each shared procedure a single canonical definition so a change propagates instead of drifting, and Scoped (FNF-4) confines every step to least-privilege tool access. Once normalized, every atomic step is a separate entity with a declared contract and can be type-checked, scope-confined, bounded, tested, traced, and audited on its own. A FAOP algebra of provably sound equalities turns refactoring and parallelization into compiler rewrites; orthogonal extensions add verified termination (+V), optimization (+O), and time and cost bounds (+B); and an architectural-level classifier (0-3) determines whether a workflow needs AI at all. Together, these make integrity, isolation, typing, termination, cost, and optimization compile-time concerns across the whole library, not runtime hopes. We implement the theory in SkillBase, an AOP management system (what PostgreSQL is to data, SkillBase is to AOPs), together with a separate executor that enforces these guarantees at run time. A worked financial workflow illustrates the approach end to end.

papers.title: Are We Testing the Wrong Quantum Bugs? A Study of Fault Representation Gaps in Quantum Software Testing
papers.summary: Quantum software relies on compilers, intermediate representations, and execution frameworks that transform programs before execution. Faults in these components can change the behavior of otherwise correct quantum programs. Yet quantum testing techniques are often evaluated using mutation-generated faults and curated bug benchmarks. We investigate how well the faults represented by these artifacts reflect those encountered in modern quantum software. We audit four quantum mutation-testing tools and three curated bug benchmarks, and collect 410 verified bugs from ten quantum software repositories over two years. We classify faults from all three sources into a common taxonomy of 56 bug families and compare their representation across mutation operators, curated benchmarks, and recent real-world bugs. The mutation tools support 20 bug families, and curated benchmarks add 15 more. Yet only 56 of the 410 real-world bugs (13.7%) belong to families represented by either source; the remaining 354 (86.3%) belong to families absent from both. The largest unrepresented families concern compiler transformations (66 bugs), type handling (53), and input validation (47). Unlike local gate or statement changes, these faults often depend on intermediate representations, compiler pipelines, input types, or dependency versions. Existing mutation operators primarily modify circuits and program constructs, whereas many real-world faults arise in the compilers, representations, and framework interfaces that process them. Addressing this gap requires looking beyond circuit-level faults toward testing semantic preservation across compiler transformations, correctness at representation boundaries, and interactions between software components. Our study provides empirical evidence to guide fault models and benchmarks that capture these mechanisms and preserve the contexts needed to reproduce them.

papers.title: MAppPrint: Robust and Real-time Mobile App Fingerprinting via Traffic Behavior Correlation Graphs
papers.summary: Mobile apps have become ubiquitous in daily life. Despite communication encryption, app fingerprinting (AF) attacks can still enable adversaries to infer the apps in use by analyzing patterns of encrypted network traffic. However, existing AF attacks suffer from three critical limitations that hinder their practical effectiveness: (i) the inability to capture app-specific traffic dependencies, rendering traffic fingerprints fragile under dynamic networking conditions; (ii) the neglect of latency and throughput considerations, resulting in inefficient real-time user tracking; and (iii) the incapacity to handle mixed traffic generated by multi-app concurrency. In this paper, we propose MAppPrint, a robust and real-time app fingerprinting framework. MAppPrint introduces a behavior-level traffic fingerprint, i.e., Traffic Behavior Correlation Graph (TBCG), which models app traffic by capturing unit traffic behaviors and their correlations, thereby providing reliable app fingerprints. To enable real-time fingerprinting, MAppPrint incorporates a fingerprint compression algorithm that transforms each TBCG into a compact graph by selectively aggregating redundant information. Furthermore, MAppPrint employs an unsupervised decomposition strategy to disentangle mixed traffic generated by multi-app concurrency, enabling unified identification of both single-app and multi-app traffic. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that MAppPrint achieves 4.9~13.9% improvement in AF precision and 3~6 times improvement in timeliness over state-of-the-art methods. Meanwhile, MAppPrint is robust in dynamic networking conditions, while achieving a throughput of 10.5 GB/s and a prediction latency of 0.68 seconds.

papers.title: Minimizing Age of Incorrect Information in Pull-Based Remote Estimation of a Markov Source
papers.summary: In this paper, we consider a discrete-time pull-based remote estimation system involving an information source and a remote monitor where the information source is a finite-state irreducible discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC) process. In this system, the remote monitor sends a pull request towards the source which responds by sampling its process so as to transmit the sampled values towards the monitor through a delay channel, encapsulated in information packets. We consider i) zero delay (ZD) and ii) unit delay (UD) channels, where the packet transmission times are zero and one slot, respectively. For remote estimation, we use the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator, and for quantifying its performance, we use the mean age of incorrect information (MAoII) which is a recently proposed freshness and mismatch metric that penalizes an incorrect estimation along with its duration. Our goal is to obtain pull policies so as to minimize MAoII under a long-run sampling rate constraint. For the ZD model, we propose a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) formulation of the problem, which allows us to find the optimum observation-dependent pull policy. On the other hand, the UD channel prevents the monitor from possessing perfect information on the actual AoII process at any given time, and the SMDP formulation of the ZD channel cannot readily be used for the UD model. For the system with the UD channel, we first provide a numerical algorithm to calculate the MAoII and the average sampling rate for a given observation-dependent pull policy. For the optimization of the underlying remote estimation system, we use the joint distribution of the age and source processes to be obtained from the history of all observations, termed as belief. Subsequently, we propose a belief-dependent policy obtained via the belief-MDP formulation and a constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) algorithm.

papers.title: X-RIC: An Agentic RAN-Intelligent Controller Benchmark for Enhancing Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: The O-RAN ALLIANCE introduces architectural flexibility through disaggregation and AI-driven control. While the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) enables centralized optimization, current AI approaches lack reasoning capabilities and explainability. We propose eXplainable RIC (X-RIC), a novel framework integrating agentic AI into O-RAN architectures. X-RIC combines reactive Reinforcement Learning (RL) with strategic agentic reasoning through: (i) automated Behavioral Cloning (BC) using domain heuristics for sample-efficient training, (ii) a Telecom Language Model (TLM), a transformer-based reasoning module providing contextual abstraction and interpretability, and (iii) closed-loop co-adaptation within the Near-RT RIC control loop enabling continuous policy refinement. To ensure deployment readiness, we introduce BARX (Benchmarking Agentic Reasoning for RAN), a domain-specific evaluation framework assessing agentic control across latency, compliance, and determinism metrics. We validate X-RIC on SLA-aware network slicing in simulation and O-RAN-compliant testbed deployments. X-RIC achieves 89% operational cost reduction while maintaining SLA compliance, converging 75% faster with 50% fewer training steps and 46% lower variance.

papers.title: ZenFlow: Enabling Stall-Free Offloading for LLM Training
papers.summary: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) often exceeds GPU memory limits, prompting systems to offload model states to CPU memory. However, existing offloaded training frameworks like ZeRO-Offload treat all parameters equally and update the full model on the CPU, causing severe GPU stalls, where fast, expensive GPUs sit idle, waiting for slow CPU updates and limited-bandwidth PCIe transfers. We present ZenFlow, a new offloaded training framework that decouples updates between GPU and CPU by prioritizing important gradients. ZenFlow performs in-place updates of important gradients on GPU while offloading and accumulating less important ones on CPU without blocking training iterations, fully overlapping CPU work with GPU computation. To make this importance-aware design scalable, ZenFlow leverages a novel spatio-temporal locality of important gradients, concentrated in specific positions that remain stable across iterations, to make important gradient identification efficient and lightweight while preserving fidelity. Evaluation shows that ZenFlow achieves up to 5x end-to-end speedup, 2x lower PCIe traffic, 85% less GPU stalls, and up to 72% lower cloud GPU cost, all while preserving accuracy.

papers.title: Asynchronous Indulgent Gathering of Opaque Robots
papers.summary: We consider the benchmarking problem of gathering in an $(N,f)$-fault system consisting of $N$ robots, of which at most $f$ may fail at any execution. The {\em traditional} version asks $N-f$ non-faulty robots to gather at a point not known a priori. The recently studied {\em indulgent} version asks $N-f$ non-faulty robots to gather at the location of a faulty one. Indulgent gathering is impossible in a $(2,1)$-crash system in the $LUMI$ model under semi-synchrony, even when infinitely many colors and coordinate axis agreement are available. In this paper, we establish four results for indulgent gathering under asynchrony in $LUMI$, considering a {\em mobility fault} model in which a robot crash only impacts its mobility but not the operation of the light. We first show that indulgent gathering is impossible in a $(2,1)$-mobility system using 2-colored lights, and then give an optimal solution w.r.t. the number of colors using 3-colored lights. We then give two deterministic algorithms for an $(N,f)$-mobility system, $f<N$, $N,f$ unknown, that exhibit a nice time-color trade-off: One with time $O(N)$ using 7-colored lights and another with time $O(\max\{\ell,f\})$ using 26-colored lights, where $\ell< N$ is the number of distinct convex layers of robot positions in the initial configuration. Our algorithms for an $(N,f)$-mobility system are the first to be analysed time complexity, can withstand obstructed visibility (opaque robot model) and asynchronous scheduling. Interestingly, our algorithms also solve traditional gathering.

papers.title: TeraAgent: A Distributed Agent-Based Simulation Engine for Simulating Half a Trillion Agents
papers.summary: Agent-based simulation is a method for studying highly complex systems in disciplines as diverse as biology, medicine, sociology, economics, finance, and more. In this method, an agent represents a small part of the system, such as a human cell, and, through interactions among many agents, the system's behavior emerges, like the growth of cancer in the human body. Real-world complex systems, such as a human organ, comprise billions of agents. However, the state-of-the-art agent-based simulation platform, BioDynaMo, does not support the distributed processing of a simulation across servers. This limitation restricts the scalability of agent counts to the computational resources available within a single server, hindering users from conducting larger and more meaningful simulations. In this paper, we introduce TeraAgent, a new distributed agent-based simulation engine. To overcome BioDynaMo's scalability limitation, TeraAgent enables efficient exchange of agent information across servers by implementing two solutions: 1) a tailored serialization mechanism that allows agents to be accessed and mutated directly at the receive buffer, and 2) delta encoding that significantly reduces data transfer across servers by leveraging the iterative nature of agent-based simulations. Built on our solutions, TeraAgent 1) enables extreme-scale simulations with half a trillion agents (292x that of BioDynaMo) on 84,096 CPU cores, 2) reduces time-to-result leveraging parallelism across compute nodes, 3) improves interoperability with third-party tools, and 4) provides users with more hardware flexibility. TeraAgent serializes agents with a median speedup of 110x (37x for deserialization) over the state-of-the-art ROOT I/O baseline, delivers 8x the agent update rate per CPU core of Biocellion, and improves in-situ visualization performance by 39x.

papers.title: How Feasible are Passive Network Attacks on 5G Networks and Beyond? A Survey
papers.summary: Privacy concerns around 5G, the latest generation of mobile networks, are growing, with fears that its deployment may increase exposure to privacy risks. This perception is largely driven by the use of denser deployments of small antenna systems, which enable highly accurate data collection at higher speeds and closer proximity to mobile users. At the same time, 5G's unique radio communication features can make the reproduction of known network attacks more challenging. In particular, passive network attacks, which do not involve direct interaction with the target network and are therefore nearly impossible to detect, remain a pressing concern. Such attacks can reveal sensitive information about users, their devices, and active applications, which may then be exploited through known vulnerabilities or spear-phishing schemes. This survey examines the feasibility of passive network attacks in 5G and beyond (B5G/6G) networks, with emphasis on two major categories: information extraction (system identification, website and application fingerprinting) and geolocation (user identification and position tracking). These attacks are well documented and reproducible in existing wireless and mobile systems, including short-range networks (IEEE 802.11) and, to a lesser extent, LTE. Current evidence suggests that while such attacks remain theoretically possible in 5G, their practical execution is significantly constrained by directional beamforming, high-frequency propagation characteristics, and encryption mechanisms. For B5G and early 6G networks, the lack of public tools and high hardware cost currently renders these attacks infeasible in practice, which highlights a critical gap in our understanding of future network threat models.

papers.title: Arcal\'{i}s: Accelerating Remote Procedure Calls Using a L\'{i}ghtweight Near-Cache Solution
papers.summary: Modern microservices increasingly depend on high-performance remote procedure calls (RPCs) to coordinate fine-grained, distributed computation. As network bandwidths continue to scale, the CPU overhead associated with RPC processing, particularly serialization, deserialization, and protocol handling, has become a critical bottleneck. This challenge is exacerbated by fast user-space networking stacks such as DPDK, which expose RPC processing as the dominant performance limiter. While prior hardware accelerators have explored NIC-attached and FPGA-based offload, these approaches remain farther from the cache hierarchy, so the frequent data accesses during RPC processing each pay an extra interconnect traversal cost that inflates RPC time. Therefore, RPC handling should occur as close as possible to the cache; however, a near-cache solution must be small, hence practical and deployable. Our key insight to enable such a solution is taking advantage of a reconfigurable accelerator that can be configured specifically for the services currently running on the CPUs. We present Arcal\'{\i}s, a near-cache RPC accelerator that positions a lightweight hardware engine adjacent to the last-level cache (LLC). Arcal\'{\i}s offloads RPC processing to dedicated microengines that operate with cache-line latency while preserving programmability. By decoupling RPC processing logic, enabling microservice-specific execution, and positioning itself near the LLC, Arcal\'{\i}s achieves a 1.72-4.91$\times$ end-to-end speedup compared to the CPU baseline, significantly reduces microarchitectural overhead by up to 88\%, and achieves up to a 1.67$\times$ higher throughput than prior solutions. These results highlight the potential of near-cache RPC acceleration as a practical solution for high-performance microservice deployment.

papers.title: A Gradual Probabilistic Lambda Calculus
papers.summary: Probabilistic programming languages extend ordinary programming languages with the ability to sample values from probability distributions. Type systems can establish invariants of such programs, for instance by assigning to a program a distribution over types that specifies the probability of each kind of outcome. However, adopting such a type discipline can be cumbersome or overly conservative. Gradual typing addresses this problem by supporting a smooth transition between static and dynamic checking, and has been successfully applied for languages with different constructs and type abstractions. Nevertheless, its benefits have never been explored in the context of probabilistic languages. In this work, we present and formalize GLANG, a gradual source probabilistic lambda calculus. GLANG includes a binary probabilistic choice operator and allows programmers to gradually introduce/remove static type---and probability---annotations. The static semantics of GLANG heavily relies on the notion of probabilistic couplings, as required for defining several relations, such as consistency, precision, and consistent transitivity. The dynamic semantics of GLANG is given via elaboration to the target language TLANG, which features a distribution-based semantics interpreting programs as probability distributions over final values. Regarding the language metatheory, we establish that TLANG---and therefore also GLANG---is type safe and satisfies two of the so-called refined criteria for gradual languages, namely, that it is a conservative extension of a fully static variant and that it satisfies (a restricted form of) the gradual guarantee, behaving smoothly with respect to type precision. The metatheory is mechanized in the Lean 4 proof assistant.

papers.title: Wattlytics: A Web Platform for Co-Optimizing Performance, Energy, and TCO in HPC Clusters
papers.summary: The escalating computational demands and energy footprint of GPU-accelerated computing systems complicate informed design and operational decisions. We present the first release of Wattlytics (https://wattlytics.netlify.app), an interactive, browser-based decision-support system. Unlike existing procurement-oriented calculators, Wattlytics uniquely integrates benchmark-driven GPU performance scaling, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)-aware piecewise power modeling, and multi-year total cost of ownership (TCO) analysis within a single interactive environment. Users can configure heterogeneous systems across contemporary GPU architectures (GH200, H100, L40S, L40, A40, A100, and L4), select representative scientific workloads (e.g., GROMACS, AMBER), and explore deployment scenarios under constraints such as energy prices, system lifetime, and frequency scaling. Wattlytics computes multidimensional decision metrics (TCO breakdown, work-per-TCO, power-per-TCO, and work-per-watt-per-TCO) and supports design-space exploration, what-if scenarios, sensitivity metrics (elasticity, Sobol indices, Monte Carlo) and collaborative features to guide realistic cluster design and procurement under uncertainty. We validate the fitted power and performance models and compare four deployment modes: fixed budget, fixed GPU count, fixed performance, and fixed power. Our case studies show that, under budget or energy constraints, optimally deployed energy-efficient GPUs can outperform higher-performance alternatives in overall cost-effectiveness. Wattlytics helps users explore the design parameter space and distinguish between cost- and risk-driving factors, turning HPC design into a well-informed and explainable decision-making process.

papers.title: TensorDex: A Compact, Tensor-Centric Storage System for Modern AI Models
papers.summary: Modern model hubs store hundreds of petabytes of large language models (LLMs), with fine-tuned variants dominating the storage footprint. These variants contain substantial cross-model redundancy that delta compression can exploit by storing only the difference between a target and a reference model. However, compression effectiveness depends critically on choosing a similar reference. At model-hub scale, this is challenging because model lineage metadata is often missing or unreliable, and different tensors within the same model may be most similar to tensors from different models. Consequently, model-level pairing leaves substantial redundancy unexploited. We present TensorDex, a lossless, tensor-centric storage system that performs delta compression at tensor granularity. TensorDex decomposes models into tensors, uses compact bit-level fingerprints to predict tensor-pair compressibility, and incrementally organizes tensors into multi-center clusters to select effective bases as new models arrive. Evaluated on 2,890 randomly sampled Hugging Face models, TensorDex reduces storage footprint by 70.5%, 37% lower than the state-of-the-art design. It achieves 22.9 GB/s compression and 28.4 GB/s decompression throughput, 3.86x and 1.49x faster than the next-best system, respectively.

papers.title: Language-Based Agent Control
papers.summary: This paper introduces language-based agent control (LBAC), a new programming model for agentic applications that brings techniques from programming languages and language-based security to the problem of agent control.
